newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK stocks hit new record despite rate fears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK stocks hit new record despite rate fears.

text.p: The British stock market leapt to a record high on Thursday, ignoring prospects of a sharp rise in interest rates after the new Labour government's first budget.
The pound remained firm -- but dipped briefly in morning trade after Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said he was not happy with the strength of sterling, which is hurting exports.
Shares had initially fallen sharply after economists said Wednesday's budget would not take the steam out of the current consumer boom and interest rates would have to rise.

But a dramatic 130-point turnaround took the FTSE 100 share index to a new all-time record high of 4,819.3 before the market steadied to hover around 4,795, up about 40 points, or 0.90 percent. The FTSE had bottomed out at 4,688.8.
Dealers said tough action on rates might look bad for securities initially, but steps to damp down future inflationary pressures would be good news for markets in the longer run.

"The average fund manager is not as gloomy as the average economist. The market is looking at the long-term positive of higher interest rates rather than the short- term negative," said Darren Winder, UK economist at SBC Warburg.

Privatised utilities led the rally as stocks rebounded from the early slump. Dealers said this sector had been let off lightly by Chancellor Gordon Brown's new windfall tax, aimed a funding a scheme to get the young unemployed back to work.

Economists said the budget was tough on business but would not quell rampant consumer demand. That would be left up to the newly-independent Bank of England, which was expected to raise interest rates, possibly by 1/2 percentage point, next week.

Some see official interest rates peaking at eight percent in the current cycle from 6.5 percent now -- a prospect which has been thrusting sterling higher and hitting the profit outlook for big British exporters such as British Steel.
Sterling hit a 61-month high of 2.9430 just after Wednesday's budget.

But Brown told reporters on Thursday he wanted to help exporters. Repeating his mantra of seeking a "strong and comptitive pound", Brown also said, "Nobody can be happy about an 18 percent rise in the pound in current circumstances."

The pound immediately fell 1/2 pfenning on Brown's comments to just above 2.93 marks. But it was not immediately clear what concrete steps the government could take to rein in sterling and the pound edged back up to around 2.9350.

On the government bond market, gilts opened sharply lower. They recovered slightly but there was no rally in this interest rate-sensitive market. Around midday, September gilts were at 114-09, down half a point from Wednesday's close.
Brown told reporters on Thursday he had produced a considerable fiscal tightening in the budget and helped bring about a better balance between fiscal and monetary policy.
But economists still believed the burden of balancing the economy was being left to monetary policy and interest rates.

"The budget...leaves the task of slowing the consumer boom to the Bank of England, meaning that interest rates are likely to rise by around 100bp (basis points) over the remainder of this year," said Paribas strategists Paul Mortimer-Lee and Nick Parsons.
The privatised utilities were a well-flagged target of the budget and shares in this sector shrugged off the impact of the new windfall tax as it turned out to be no worse than expected.
Airport authority BAA was up 20-1/2 pence at 593 pence and Railtrack Railtrack soared 40 to 672.
Shares in British Telecommunications Plc BT.L) leapt seven percent to a new record of 490 pence, before easing back to around 478 pence, a rise of 20-1/2 pence.
"They seem to have got off lightly" said one trader. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
